edition.title: P100 NEWS + CULTURE + SCIENCE & TECH + SPORT
edition.deck: Fresh developments span attacks on Saudi Arabia, an uncertain Ukraine ceasefire, UK political and budget disputes, and Danish security and household costs.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritise consequential developments and preserve what remains unverified. Group reports on the same events; distinguish confirmed facts from allegations, forecasts and political claims.

content.headline: Saudi Arabia vows ‘serious response’ after deadly Houthi airport attacks
content.shortHeadline: Saudi Arabia vows response after deadly airport attacks
content.standfirst: Repeated strikes have hit airports and other targets in the kingdom, including two terminals at Riyadh’s main airport. The attacks have killed people and raised the risk of a wider regional escalation.

image.caption: Security-camera footage shows the moment a strike hit a terminal at Riyadh airport.

sources.originalTitle: Saudi minister vows 'serious response' to Houthi attacks on airports
Houthi-angreb rammer Saudi-Arabien, hvor det gør særligt ondt, vurderer forsker

segments.body: Saudi Arabia’s energy minister has vowed a “serious” response to Houthi attacks on airports and energy facilities. A Pakistani man was killed when a projectile hit a terminal at Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on Sunday, a day after a strike there killed 13 people, Saudi authorities said.

segments.title: A wider regional risk
segments.body: The Houthis say the attacks are retaliation for Saudi actions in Yemen, where a Saudi-led coalition supports pro-government forces. Saudi Arabia says its forces intercepted other missiles and drones. A researcher quoted by DR says the strikes also threaten the kingdom’s efforts to attract tourists and investors.

perspectives.body: Roskilde University researcher Fannie Agerschou-Madsen says attacks on Riyadh’s airport strike at a prominent part of Saudi Arabia’s bid to attract visitors and foreign investment, as well as hitting targets far from Yemen.

content.headline: Ukraine says Russian strikes continue as Trump announces an unconfirmed energy ‘
content.shortHeadline: Ukraine says Russian strikes continue after Trump’s ceasefire claim
content.standfirst: Donald Trump said Russia and Ukraine had agreed to halt attacks on energy sites, but Kyiv says it was not consulted and reports fresh Russian strikes. Moscow has not confirmed an agreement.

image.caption: Cars burn after a Russian strike on a residential neighbourhood in Kharkiv.

sources.originalTitle: Zelenskyy vows to retaliate if Russian strikes on Ukraine’s power grid continue
Trump declared a surprise ‘energy ceasefire’ in Ukraine. Here’s how it’s going
Trump siger, at våbenhvile er på plads – Zelenskyj blev dog overrasket
Trump faces growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia
Explainer: Det har været en hård weekend for Ukraine – 'nu er vi på kollisionskurs'

segments.body: Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine would retaliate if Russian attacks on its power grid continue. He said he was surprised by Donald Trump’s announcement of an energy ceasefire and that neither side had agreed to the terms. Russia launched drone attacks on Kyiv and struck energy facilities, Zelenskyy said.

segments.title: Diesel deal adds to the dispute
segments.body: The ceasefire claim follows Trump’s announcement that Russia would supply diesel to the US and global markets, alongside a temporary suspension of sanctions on Russian diesel exports, according to the BBC. Seven US senators from both parties say the deal violates US law; Trump’s administration disputes that interpretation. The promised quantities and their effect on fuel prices remain uncertain.

perspectives.body: DR’s account emphasises that the proposed diesel volumes are small compared with US demand, while arguing that the deal could still bring revenue to Russia and weaken pressure on Moscow. It also describes possible US pressure on Ukraine and its European allies.

content.headline: Cyber-attack makes refrigeration systems heat up in French supermarkets
content.shortHeadline: French supermarket cyber-attack spoils chilled and frozen food
content.standfirst: Hackers interfered with refrigeration systems at several major chains, forcing stores to discard affected food. Prosecutors have opened an investigation; the full scale of the attack and losses is not yet known.

image.caption: Food retailers say affected branches must discard fresh and frozen products after refrigeration systems were tampered with.

sources.originalTitle: Fridges in French supermarkets hit by cyber attack
Cyber-attack defrosts refrigerators in two French supermarket chains
Temperaturer blev skruet op under cyberangreb i franske supermarkeder

segments.body: A cyber-attack caused refrigerators and freezers at French supermarkets to heat up, spoiling fresh and frozen food. Intermarché and Coopérative U reported affected stores, and the Paris prosecutor’s office has opened an investigation into what it called a large-scale attack on several food retailers.

segments.title: Scale remains unclear
segments.body: Reports differ on the number of affected branches: the BBC cites more than 100 Coopérative U stores and at least 300 Intermarché and Netto stores, while the Guardian reports nearly 100 Coopérative U outlets and 150–200 Intermarché shops. Some local reports name other chains, but their involvement has not been confirmed by all retailers. The total food losses and financial damage are unknown.

content.headline: BBC investigation alleges falsified records hid Roman Abramovich’s wealth
content.shortHeadline: BBC alleges falsified records concealed Abramovich’s wealth
content.standfirst: A BBC Panorama investigation says backdated paperwork helped remove assets from company accounts and avoid tax in Cyprus. Abramovich denies wrongdoing, and Deloitte says it cannot comment on specific allegations.

image.caption: Leaked documents examined in a BBC investigation into Roman Abramovich’s finances.

sources.originalTitle: Documents falsified to evade tax on Abramovich's wealth, BBC finds

segments.body: A joint investigation by BBC Panorama and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism alleges that backdated documents were used to hide Roman Abramovich’s wealth and evade tax. It says Deloitte Cyprus signed off accounts that made $672m of assets disappear from one company’s published accounts, and found evidence of altered records relating to interest income and a larger company fortune.

segments.title: Denials and unanswered questions
segments.body: Abramovich’s lawyers say he denies evading tax or concealing his fortune, and that there is no evidence he knew about or directed the falsification of documents. Deloitte Cyprus says it acts in compliance with applicable laws and cannot comment on specific allegations because the documents are more than 20 years old and no longer accessible. The report is based on leaked records; it does not establish a court finding of wrongdoing.

content.headline: US agents search Congresswoman Ilhan Omar’s home in criminal investigation
content.shortHeadline: US agents search Ilhan Omar’s home in criminal investigation
content.standfirst: The Justice Department says the search was authorised by a warrant but has not explained the investigation. The timing, weeks before the midterm elections, is likely to draw scrutiny; Omar has not commented on the search.

sources.originalTitle: Immigration agents search Congresswoman Ilhan Omar's home

segments.body: Homeland Security Investigations agents searched the Washington-area home of Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar on Monday under a judicially authorised warrant, a Justice Department spokesperson told the BBC. The department described the matter as an ongoing federal criminal investigation but gave no further details. It is unclear whether Omar was at the home.

segments.title: Investigation not specified
segments.body: Omar, a Democrat seeking re-election, has previously denied separate allegations about her immigration records made by Republican politicians. The BBC reports that the nature of Monday’s investigation remains unclear and that it has contacted Omar for comment. The search came 22 days before the midterm elections.

content.headline: Pupil arrested after shooting injures two staff at school in southern France
content.shortHeadline: Two staff injured in shooting at French school; pupil arrested
content.standfirst: A 14-year-old pupil was arrested after a head teacher and another teacher were shot at a school near Marseille. Officials say their injuries are not life-threatening; the motive remains unclear.

image.caption: Police at the school in Aubagne after the shooting on Monday.

sources.originalTitle: Pupil arrested after two teachers shot at French school
Rektor og skolelærer skudt i Frankrig

segments.body: A 14-year-old pupil was arrested after a head teacher and a teacher were shot at Lakanal middle school in Aubagne, near Marseille, on Monday. The teachers’ injuries are not life-threatening, officials said; no pupils were injured. The suspect was restrained by a member of staff, and prosecutors have opened an attempted-murder investigation.

The Marseille prosecutor said the pupil fired in a classroom after injuring the two staff members. A third person was reportedly grazed, according to the brief account from DR. The motive has not been established, and local media reported the incident was not thought to be linked to school-condition protests.

content.headline: US detains Colombian man accused of laundering money from Venezuelan schemes
content.shortHeadline: US detains Colombian man accused in Venezuelan money-laundering cases
content.standfirst: Álvaro Pulido is accused by US prosecutors of laundering more than $2bn in Venezuelan government bribery schemes. He is due in court on Tuesday; the allegations have not been tested at trial.

image.caption: Álvaro Pulido, whom US authorities sought over money-laundering indictments.

sources.originalTitle: US detains man accused in multi-billion Venezuelan money laundering scheme

segments.body: Colombian businessman Álvaro Pulido has been detained in the United States in a Homeland Security Task Force operation, the Justice Department said. US prosecutors accuse him of laundering more than $2bn connected to Venezuelan government bribery schemes and say he worked with former Venezuelan official Alex Saab. Pulido is due in court on Tuesday.

The indictments allege that Pulido and co-defendants bribed officials to win contracts to provide food and medicine, then moved profits through overseas bank accounts. Prosecutors also accuse him and Saab of laundering $350m in a separate currency-exchange scheme. The charges are allegations, and the report gives no response from Pulido.

content.headline: India protests resume after court releases three leaders of Cockroach Janta
content.shortHeadline: India protest leaders released as demonstrations are expected to grow
content.standfirst: Three leaders of the Cockroach Janta Party were released after a court order, as authorities prepared for further demonstrations in New Delhi. Protesters allege names were removed from voter lists; the election commission denies the charge.

sources.originalTitle: Indiens Kakerlak-ledere løsladt – politi forbereder sig på nyt kaos

segments.body: Three leaders of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), detained while preparing a protest in New Delhi, were released by court order, according to their lawyer. Authorities deployed thousands of security personnel and closed roads ahead of further demonstrations, which follow a protest against changes to India’s voter lists.

The movement says hundreds of millions of names may have been removed from voter lists and is demanding an independent investigation and the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. The election commission rejects the allegations. The terms of the leaders’ release, including whether they may protest, were not clear in the report.

content.headline: Reform proposes five-year asylum shutdown and mass deportations
content.shortHeadline: Reform proposes asylum shutdown and mass deportations
content.standfirst: Nigel Farage’s party says it would reject new asylum claims, review some existing cases and deport people, including families. Refugee groups call the proposals unworkable; legal, diplomatic and practical obstacles remain.

image.caption: Nigel Farage announced Reform UK’s proposed asylum and deportation policy.

sources.originalTitle: Children and mothers included in Reform plan to immediately deport 90,000 asylum seekers
The four major flaws in Reform’s plan to shut down asylum system

segments.body: Reform UK says it would close the asylum system to new claims for five years, void existing applications and seek to deport people to their home countries or a “safe” third country. The plan would not exempt children and mothers, Nigel Farage said. The party says it would review people granted asylum since 2024, while keeping routes for Ukrainians.

segments.title: Questions over implementation
segments.body: The party proposes using visa restrictions, tariffs and other measures to pressure countries to accept deportees, but the i Paper notes that tariffs could breach World Trade Organization rules. Third-country agreements, detention space and changes to UK law and international treaty commitments would also be required. The Refugee Council says the proposals would cause chaos and drive people underground.

content.headline: IFS says Healey may need £35bn to meet Budget pledges without cuts
content.shortHeadline: IFS warns Healey faces £35bn Budget gap
content.standfirst: The Institute for Fiscal Studies says higher inflation and planned defence spending could force the chancellor to choose between service cuts, tax rises or a changed timetable. Its forecasts are exceptionally uncertain ahead of the 28 October Budget.

sources.originalTitle: Healey faces £35bn Budget challenge to meet spending pledges, says think tank
The tax rises that could come in the Budget – and how likely they are
What the Budget could mean for state pensions, private pots and lump sums

segments.body: Chancellor John Healey may need to find about £35bn if the government wants to raise defence spending to 3% of national income by 2030 and increase health spending without squeezing other departments, the Institute for Fiscal Studies says. Higher inflation linked to the Iran war could further erode departments’ budgets.

segments.title: Choices and uncertainty
segments.body: The IFS says the chancellor must set out credible plans rather than rely on future spending cuts he may not deliver. Options being discussed include tax changes, but the government has promised not to raise income tax, VAT or employee National Insurance on working people. The IFS warns its forecasts are exceptionally uncertain, and the official forecast could differ.

perspectives.body: The i Paper’s Budget analysis outlines possible measures including changes to capital gains tax, pension tax relief and the tax-free pension lump sum. These remain options under discussion, not announced Budget decisions.

content.headline: Burnham renews EU reset push and says Russia interfered in Brexit vote
content.shortHeadline: Burnham revives EU reset and Russia interference claims
content.standfirst: The prime minister says he received a “clear answer” that Russia interfered in the 2016 referendum, but has not named the source or evidence. He is also urging closer EU ties, reopening political disputes over Brexit.

image.caption: Andy Burnham, who has said he was told Russia interfered in the Brexit referendum.

sources.originalTitle: How significant are Burnham’s remarks on Kremlin interference in Brexit vote?
Rusland blandede sig i Brexit-afstemning, siger premierminister
Burnham: not pursuing better EU deal would be ‘dereliction of duty’

segments.body: Andy Burnham says he was told after entering Downing Street that Russia interfered in the 2016 Brexit referendum. He has not said who gave him that answer or what it was based on. A parliamentary intelligence committee previously said the government had not sought or seen evidence of successful interference and that no formal post-referendum assessment had been made.

segments.title: A renewed argument over Europe
segments.body: Burnham is also urging MPs to pursue closer cooperation with the EU, arguing that failing to seek a better deal would be a dereliction of duty. His proposals have prompted concern among some Labour MPs from leave-voting constituencies and opposition from Conservatives. Downing Street says it regards the referendum result as legitimate.

perspectives.body: The Guardian reports that Burnham’s planned Commons statement is intended to press for practical cooperation on trade and migration, while some of his own MPs fear reopening Brexit divisions.

content.headline: SAS personnel refuse inquiry questions on alleged Afghanistan killings
content.shortHeadline: SAS personnel refuse inquiry questions on alleged Afghanistan killings
content.standfirst: The judge-led inquiry says a high proportion of SAS personnel asked for evidence have invoked their right against self-incrimination. Investigators are examining allegations of more than 50 killings and a possible cover-up; no findings have yet been made.

image.caption: The inquiry is examining allegations of killings by a UK special forces unit in Afghanistan.

sources.originalTitle: SAS personnel ‘refusing to answer’ questions about alleged extrajudicial killings in Afghanistan

segments.body: Most SAS personnel approached by the inquiry into alleged unlawful killings in Afghanistan have refused to answer questions, its chair, Lord Justice Haddon-Cave, told a public hearing. The inquiry is examining allegations that 54 Afghans were killed in suspicious circumstances by one unit in Helmand province in 2010 and 2011.

segments.title: Evidence still being gathered
segments.body: The inquiry is examining whether military police investigations were effective, whether killings occurred between 2010 and 2013, and whether evidence was covered up. Haddon-Cave said it had obtained about 10,000 high-resolution photographs from detention operations that do not appear to have formed part of earlier police inquiries. The allegations remain under investigation.

content.headline: UK minister says AI cyber-attack on government systems is ‘likely’
content.shortHeadline: UK minister warns AI cyber-attack is ‘likely, if not inevitable’
content.standfirst: AI minister Kanishka Narayan says the UK must prepare for cyber defences to be breached, after an AI agent accessed an Australian government website. The government plans to use AI to identify vulnerabilities and strengthen protections.

image.caption: AI minister Kanishka Narayan has warned that UK cyber defences could be breached.

sources.originalTitle: AI minister warns 'likely' UK's cyber defences will be breached
Cyber-attack like OpenAI Medicare breach ‘seems likely’ in UK, says minister

segments.body: Kanishka Narayan said it was “likely, if not inevitable” that UK cyber defences would be breached. He pointed to an incident in which an AI agent accessed an Australian government website; Australian authorities say no personal medical records are known to have been accessed and there is no evidence of wider compromise.

segments.title: Preparing for the risk
segments.body: The government plans to use advanced AI to help find and fix vulnerabilities in public systems, building on pilots that Narayan says have identified more than 1,000. He also says the UK’s AI Security Institute is evaluating advanced models before release, after the government worked with the US to retain access to them.

content.headline: New chronic UTI definition could be ready in early 2027, campaigners say
content.shortHeadline: Experts aim to define chronic UTIs by early 2027
content.standfirst: Clinicians are working towards a shared definition of chronic urinary tract infections, which campaigners say could improve diagnosis and treatment. The process is still under way, and better diagnostic tools and research remain key demands.

sources.originalTitle: How chronic UTI sufferers could finally have official medical condition by 2027

segments.body: A panel of clinicians is using a consensus process to develop a clinical definition of chronic urinary tract infections, with GP Cat Anderson hoping it will be ready in early 2027. Campaigners say the condition is difficult to diagnose and that existing urine tests can miss infections.

segments.title: Recognition is not a treatment
segments.body: A shared definition could support clinical guidance and further research, but it would not itself resolve patients’ difficulties accessing care. Patients and clinicians quoted by the i Paper call for more accurate diagnostic tools and treatment options, and say care should reflect both clinical evidence and patient experience. The proposed definition has not yet been finalised.

content.headline: Government launches flood taskforce as millions face risk this winter
content.shortHeadline: Flood taskforce launched as millions face risk this winter
content.standfirst: The Met Office sees an increased chance of wetter-than-usual conditions in late autumn and early winter, but cannot predict where flooding will occur. The new taskforce will focus on preparations, even as much of England remains in drought.

sources.originalTitle: The areas most at risk of flash floods as El Niño threatens millions in UK

segments.body: The government is establishing a Flood and Drought Resilience Taskforce as the Met Office warns of a greater likelihood of wetter-than-normal conditions later this autumn and early winter. The Environment Agency says 6.3 million homes and businesses in England are at risk of flooding; the forecast does not identify which places will be affected this year.

segments.title: Flood risk and drought can coexist
segments.body: The taskforce is due to bring together more than 50 organisations and will be accompanied by online advice for households. The i Paper reports that more than two-thirds of England remains in drought after the hot, dry summer. A single intense downpour can cause surface-water flooding even while longer-term drought continues.

content.headline: Boarding schools urged to strengthen response to pupil-on-pupil sexual abuse
content.shortHeadline: Boarding schools face calls to strengthen abuse safeguards
content.standfirst: Survivors and safeguarding specialists say children living at school can face distinct risks and need trusted routes to report abuse. Schools and sector representatives say training and procedures have improved, but the adequacy of responses remains under scrutiny.

sources.originalTitle: Why boarding schools must do more to tackle child-on-child sexual abuse

segments.body: Two former boarding pupils described sexual abuse by other students and the lasting effects of what happened. In one case, a pupil was convicted of offences against two boys; in another, a family brought a civil claim against a school, which denied liability before a settlement was reached. The Guardian reports that abuse between pupils is receiving greater scrutiny.

segments.title: Duty to act
segments.body: A victims’ organisation says policies alone are not enough and that pupils need safe routes to disclose abuse, with responses that put their welfare ahead of institutional reputation. The Boarding Schools’ Association says schools have strengthened training and safeguarding guidance. Experts quoted in the report stress that schools must be prepared to investigate concerns and protect children.

content.headline: Danish tax inquiry projected to cost nearly half a billion kroner
content.shortHeadline: Danish tax inquiry costs projected to reach DKK 467m
content.standfirst: A commission examining tax-collection failures and the dividend-tax fraud case is budgeted to cost DKK 467.3m over ten years. It expects to finish its report in late 2026 or early 2027, after receiving tens of millions of files.

image.caption: The commission, established in 2017, is examining problems in the former tax authority.

sources.originalTitle: Udgifter til undersøgelse af Skat nærmer sig en halv milliard kroner

segments.body: The state’s projected bill for the commission investigating problems in the former tax authority, Skat, has risen to DKK 467.3m, according to a new budget estimate sent to parliament. The inquiry, established in 2017, also examines the dividend-tax case in which Danish authorities were defrauded of billions in tax refunds.

segments.title: A long-running inquiry
segments.body: The commission has received more than 56 million electronic files and conducted 268 hearings, according to DR. It expects to complete the report’s final chapters in the second half of 2026 and early 2027. The latest estimate is up from nearly DKK 400m a year ago.

content.headline: Making Denmark’s public shelters ready could cost up to DKK 3bn
content.shortHeadline: Denmark’s public shelters could cost up to DKK 3bn to prepare
content.standfirst: An estimate puts the cost of refurbishing all 1,694 public concrete shelters at DKK 2bn–3bn, with substantial uncertainty. Repairing the 831 that already meet basic requirements could cost DKK 500m–1bn.

image.caption: A public concrete shelter in Denmark, one of the types included in the refurbishment estimate.

sources.originalTitle: Klargøring af 1694 beskyttelsesrum kan koste op mod tre milliarder

segments.body: Preparing all 1,694 of Denmark’s publicly accessible concrete shelters for use could cost between DKK 2bn and DKK 3bn, emergency-preparedness minister Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen said in a parliamentary response. The estimates are uncertain and would need further assessment.

The ministry estimates that work on the 831 shelters already meeting basic requirements could cost DKK 500m–1bn. Many shelters need treatment for mould and pests after years without use. An inspection of other types of shelters is still under way and is expected to finish in 2027.

content.headline: Danish MPs back compensation for neighbours of planned ammunition factory
content.shortHeadline: Danish politicians call for help for ammunition-factory neighbours
content.standfirst: Politicians from several parties say residents near a planned explosives factory in Elling should receive compensation or have the option to sell their homes. Some residents say money alone cannot address their safety concerns.

sources.originalTitle: ’En opgave, de tager på sig på nationens vegne’: Flere partier vil hjælpe naboer til krudtfabrik

segments.body: Politicians from both government and opposition parties say residents near the planned ammunition factory in Elling should receive compensation, amid concerns about safety, possible sabotage and falling property values. The legal options are still being examined, and it is not settled whether the state will compensate residents or buy their homes.

Resident Jan Vestergaard says he would prefer the state to buy his home, arguing that no sum can put a value on his family’s safety. Conservative defence spokesperson Marcus Knuth says an independent assessment is needed and that buying some homes could be an option.

content.headline: US military orders DKK 534m in missile-tracking radars from Danish firm
content.shortHeadline: US military orders DKK 534m of radars from Danish company
content.standfirst: Weibel Scientific in Allerød will supply six radars designed to track moving objects such as ballistic missiles and aircraft. The company’s director says the order shows Danish industry can compete in defence technology.

image.caption: Weibel Scientific’s radar technology is designed to track missiles and aircraft.

sources.originalTitle: Stor amerikansk militærordre til dansk forsvarsvirksomhed

segments.body: The US military has ordered six radars from Danish company Weibel Scientific for DKK 534m. The company says the equipment can measure the movement and position of objects including ballistic missiles and fighter aircraft with high precision.

Weibel’s chief executive says the order should encourage Danish policymakers to factor domestic industry into a national defence strategy. A financial analyst quoted by TV 2 sees the contract as evidence that US-European defence ties continue despite wider political tensions.

content.headline: District-heating bills set to rise as providers face energy and grid constraints
content.shortHeadline: District-heating bills to rise as energy costs and grid limits bite
content.standfirst: Several Danish providers have announced increases for next year, including a 40% rise in Præstø. Its utility says limited access to electricity has forced it back to gas, while the industry warns prices may rise more widely.

image.caption: District-heating customers in several parts of Denmark are facing higher prices.

sources.originalTitle: Kæmpe stigninger i fjernvarmepriserne rammer

segments.body: District-heating prices are set to rise in several parts of Denmark. Præstø residents face a 40% increase from 2027; reported rises elsewhere include 32% in Sønder Felding and 18% in Svendborg. The increases come after district-heating prices rose about 30% nationally over five years, according to TV 2.

segments.title: Electricity access limits cheaper production
segments.body: Præstø Fjernvarme says it has been disconnected from the electricity grid 67 times this year and has had to return to gas after successfully electrifying production. The company says it may wait 48 months for a permanent grid connection. Industry representatives say providers use different energy sources and the impact on bills will vary.

content.headline: Sorø teachers use screen-monitoring software to keep pupils focused
content.shortHeadline: Screen-monitoring software helps Sorø teachers keep pupils on task
content.standfirst: Teachers in Sorø can view pupils’ school-computer screens and block distracting sites. A lecturer says the tools may help concentration but warns against constant surveillance; pupils describe both discomfort and benefits.

image.caption: A pupil at Borgerskolen in Sorø, where teachers use software to monitor school-computer activity.

sources.originalTitle: Fuld kontrol over skærmene: En 'lidt ubehagelig' løsning gør, at eleverne lærer mere

segments.body: Teachers at a school in Sorø use LanSchool and Netsweeper to block distracting content and see what pupils are doing on school computers. Teacher Rasmus Thomsen says the programmes help him ensure pupils are working on assigned tasks, after some used school devices for games and social media.

segments.title: Focus and privacy
segments.body: Some pupils say being visible to teachers feels uncomfortable, while also making it easier to concentrate. Aarhus University lecturer Andreas Lieberoth says awareness that activity can be seen may help, but cautions against turning classrooms into places of constant surveillance. The school describes the software as a classroom-management tool, not surveillance.

content.headline: Train disruption between Odense and Fredericia expected to last all week
content.shortHeadline: Train disruption between Odense and Fredericia to last all week
content.standfirst: Regional trains on the route are replaced by buses through 18 October, while some other services run more slowly. A fire at signalling equipment near Aarup is causing ongoing faults; a fallen tree also halted services earlier on Monday.

sources.originalTitle: Rejsende med DSB kan forvente længere køretid i hele uge 42

segments.body: Passengers travelling between Odense and Fredericia should expect longer journeys through Sunday 18 October, DSB says. Regional trains are replaced by buses, while international trains and InterCity services continue, in some cases at lower speeds.

The disruption follows a fire at a signalling hut near Aarup on Friday, which caused signal faults between Middelfart and Odense. A fallen tree also stopped trains in both directions early Monday; InterCity services resumed around 06:00, but regional trains remain replaced by buses.

content.headline: Police withdraw fines wrongly issued to parents over children’s e-scooter use
content.shortHeadline: Police withdraw wrongly issued e-scooter fines to parents
content.standfirst: East Jutland Police say they issued fines without legal authority in 12 cases involving children under 15 riding e-scooters unaccompanied. The force says affected families will be notified and procedures reviewed.

sources.originalTitle: Politi trækker bøder tilbage efter fejl

segments.body: East Jutland Police say they wrongly issued DKK 1,000 fines to parents in 12 cases involving children under 15 riding e-scooters without an adult. The force says there was no legal basis for the fines and that it will contact the affected families in the coming days.

There were 19 cases in total: in seven, police issued charges but no fines. The force says it regrets the mistake and has reviewed its procedures. Any scooters that were illegal remain confiscated, according to police.

content.headline: Fontaines D.C.’s Dopamine Chamber turns modern dread into a grand triumph
content.shortHeadline: Fontaines D.C. turn modern dread into a grand triumph
content.standfirst: On their fifth album, the Dublin band pair Grian Chatten’s unsettling questions about truth and desire with music that is lavish, seductive and assured. The Guardian’s reviewer calls it their most formidable record yet.

image.caption: Fontaines D.C. performing.

sources.originalTitle: Fontaines DC: Dopamine Chamber review – gloomy, gorgeous and a gargantuan triumph

segments.body: Fontaines D.C.’s fifth album, Dopamine Chamber, channels anxieties about social media, artificial intelligence and the erosion of truth into darkly alluring songs. Chatten’s lyrics question desire and reality, while the band’s expansive arrangements make the record’s ominous ideas feel thrilling rather than oppressive.

segments.title: Ambition with substance
segments.body: The review hears the band’s arena-sized ambition matched by songs with enough detail and force to sustain it. Rosalía’s appearance on the dramatic duet “Where Is Gone?” is singled out as a highlight; the album’s confidence, the critic argues, helps Fontaines D.C. sound like a band comfortable with its scale.

content.headline: Jay-Z in 8 had the makings of a probing documentary. It settles for praise
content.shortHeadline: Jay-Z’s documentary leaves the hard questions unasked
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s critic argues that Rick Rubin’s eight-part conversation with Jay-Z gives the rapper room to shape his public image but rarely challenges him. The result, they say, is a missed chance to examine the tensions between his politics and his billionaire status.

image.caption: Jay-Z and Rick Rubin in Jay-Z in 8.

sources.originalTitle: The missed opportunity of Jay-Z’s documentary series

segments.body: Jay-Z in 8 traces the rapper’s music and life through conversations with producer Rick Rubin. The series includes recollections of family, songwriting and difficult personal history, but the Guardian review argues that Rubin’s approving approach leaves the central questions largely untouched.

segments.title: Control without confrontation
segments.body: The review focuses on the gap between Jay-Z’s reflections on inequality and social movements and his position as one of the world’s richest musicians. It argues that a more searching interviewer might have tested those contradictions, as well as Jay-Z’s desire to control the stories told about him. Rubin’s restraint, the critic concludes, turns a potentially revealing music documentary into hagiography.

content.headline: Grouper’s Liz Harris explains why streaming success can feel unsafe
content.shortHeadline: Grouper’s Liz Harris on streaming scams and collaboration
content.standfirst: After a Grouper song went viral, fraudsters tried to claim its royalties. In a wide-ranging interview, Liz Harris describes the risks of online music platforms—and how making a record with her band Helen offered a restorative counterweight to working alone.

image.caption: Liz Harris of Grouper and Helen.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s rational to fear the music industry’: Grouper’s Liz Harris on virality, streaming scammers and her ‘restorative’ dream-pop trio

segments.body: Liz Harris, who records as Grouper, says a viral resurgence of her song “Poison Tree” brought a practical threat: someone had fraudulently uploaded and registered the track, claiming royalties. Harris and her label were able to stop the scam and recover what she was owed, but she says that policing fake uploads and remixes consumes artists’ time.

segments.title: The value of making music together
segments.body: The interview also explores Harris’s return to Helen, the dream-pop trio she shares with Jed Bindeman and Scott Simmons. She describes the group’s collaborative process as restorative, a source of friendship and shared energy that differs from the solitary work of Grouper. The contrast gives the conversation a broader portrait of an artist wary of the music business but still drawn to community.

content.headline: Marc Almond says Soft Cell’s final album became a farewell to Dave Ball
content.shortHeadline: Marc Almond on Soft Cell’s final album and Dave Ball
content.standfirst: Soft Cell had finished Danceteria when keyboardist Dave Ball died two days later, Marc Almond recalls. The singer describes the album as a closing chapter shaped by their early-1980s New York experiences and the long creative partnership behind the duo.

image.caption: Marc Almond and Dave Ball of Soft Cell.

sources.originalTitle: Soft Cell’s Marc Almond: ‘We finished the album – two days later Dave passed away’

segments.body: Marc Almond says he and Dave Ball agreed that Soft Cell’s new record, Danceteria, was finished shortly before Ball died in October 2025. Almond says he would not make another Soft Cell album without his bandmate, making this their sixth and final record.

segments.title: A New York story
segments.body: The album revisits the duo’s time in early-1980s New York, drawing on its nightlife and creative freedom as well as the loneliness and fear that came with the AIDS crisis. Almond describes the record as a fitting end to a relationship that lasted almost 50 years, saying the two had become closer while making it.

content.headline: Jamie T says rising costs have put touring Europe out of reach
content.shortHeadline: Jamie T says Europe tours no longer add up financially
content.standfirst: As he releases Ghosts (100 Days of Morning), Jamie T reflects on panic disorder, the early days of his career and the songs that look back on them. He says the cost of taking his band to Europe has so far made a tour financially unworkable.

image.caption: Jamie T.

sources.originalTitle: Jamie T: ‘I can’t afford to tour Europe anymore’

segments.body: Jamie T says he cannot currently make the numbers work for a European tour with his band. He would like to take his new album, Ghosts (100 Days of Morning), beyond the UK, but says touring costs are high and the plans are not adding up. He describes the situation as frustrating, while noting that ticket sales are a major source of income.

segments.title: Writing through anxiety
segments.body: The interview revisits Treays’s long experience of panic disorder and his reflections on growing up in public after his debut album, Panic Prevention. He says the new record looks back at those earlier years in the hope of tying them up and moving on, while he now feels in better shape than during the most difficult period of his touring career.

content.headline: Tom Morello’s first solo rock album turns protest into a family story
content.shortHeadline: Tom Morello’s solo album is a protest record—and a family story
content.standfirst: On Everyone Gets What They Want, the Rage Against the Machine guitarist brings his anti-racist and anti-fascist politics into a first full-length solo rock record. He also credits his mother’s activism—and his son Roman’s musical ideas—as formative influences.

image.caption: Tom Morello.

sources.originalTitle: Tom Morello on Rage Against the Machine fans turning against him

segments.body: Tom Morello describes his first full-length solo rock album, Everyone Gets What They Want, as a record for people opposed to racism and fascism. The interview presents it as a continuation of his long use of music as activism, with songs featuring guests including Serj Tankian and Kneecap.

segments.title: A legacy of action
segments.body: Morello says his mother, Mary, taught him that ordinary people can help change the world. He recalls her work against racism and for workers, and has established a memorial project in her name. His son Roman, 15, co-wrote five songs on the album; Morello describes their musical collaboration as a source of joy.

content.headline: Dawn Richard’s Creole culture celebrates New Orleans in motion
content.shortHeadline: Dawn Richard celebrates New Orleans on Creole culture
content.standfirst: The final album in Dawn Richard’s trilogy devoted to her hometown draws on New Orleans styles through live playing, programmed beats and fluid transitions. Pitchfork praises its communal energy while noting that its grounded approach is less adventurous than her strongest work.

sources.originalTitle: creole culture

segments.body: On Creole culture, Dawn Richard brings her New Orleans roots to the end of a trilogy that began with 2019’s new breed. The album mixes styles and live instrumentation in songs that move between jazz, bounce, reggae, gospel, amapiano and electronic production, presenting the city as communal and constantly in motion.

segments.title: A quieter kind of experiment
segments.body: Pitchfork hears an intimate approach to cultural influence rather than a bid for novelty, with Richard sounding at home across the album’s changing styles. The review also finds the songwriting less daring than her earlier work, but says the record’s homespun pride and sense of movement remain appealing.

content.headline: Cameron Winter’s Carnegie Hall album turns a concert into a legend
content.shortHeadline: Cameron Winter’s Carnegie Hall set captures a star in the making
content.standfirst: A solo recording from Geese frontman Cameron Winter’s Carnegie Hall performance foregrounds new songs, piano playing and the risks of a live performance. Pitchfork hears the beginnings of a repertoire that could outlast the night itself.

sources.originalTitle: Live at Carnegie Hall

segments.body: Live at Carnegie Hall documents Cameron Winter’s December 2025 solo concert, including three unreleased songs and an appearance by film-makers Paul Thomas Anderson and Benny Safdie during “Nina + Field of Cops”. The review hears Winter’s piano arrangements open up songs that felt more constrained on his studio debut, Heavy Metal.

segments.title: A performance, and its mythology
segments.body: Pitchfork praises Winter’s new material and the unsettled intensity of his singing, while recognising that the concert recording and accompanying film also build a story around a young artist’s rise. The critic sees the live versions transforming difficult, personal songs into performances that feel larger than their creator.

content.headline: Why British films keep returning to rebellions that failed
content.shortHeadline: British cinema keeps returning to failed rebellions
content.standfirst: Paul Greengrass’s The Uprising joins a small group of British films about crushed collective action. A Guardian essay argues that the country’s cinema more readily romanticises military defeat than confronts its history of revolutionary struggles.

image.caption: Andrew Garfield in The Uprising.

sources.originalTitle: Mort à la révolution! Why UK film loves a failed rebellion

segments.body: Paul Greengrass’s The Uprising, about the 1381 Peasants’ Revolt, is an unusually direct attempt to bring a failed popular uprising into British cinema. The Guardian’s essay places it alongside films such as Winstanley, Comrades and Peterloo, arguing that British movies have often neglected revolutionary defeats even as they revisit other national failures.

segments.title: The limits of the everyman
segments.body: The essay welcomes the film’s attention to class conflict but argues that it turns collective action into an individual hero’s story, and questions its suggestion of a link to Robin Hood. It sees this as a tension between the film’s political subject and the conventions it borrows from Hollywood, where struggles are often framed through individual freedom rather than collective goals.

segments.title: A national story still contested
segments.body: The piece contrasts British retellings of failure with the more frequent revolutionary stories in American, French and Irish cinema. It argues that the absence of British films about movements such as Chartism reflects a narrower idea of what counts as heroic history, and connects the subject to present-day inequality and distrust of political leaders.

content.headline: A Fidai Film reclaims Palestinian archive footage from historical erasure
content.shortHeadline: A Fidai Film turns suppressed Palestinian footage into art
content.standfirst: Kamal Aljafari’s collage documentary reworks archival footage of Palestinian life and violence, some of it taken from a Beirut research centre raided in 1982. The Guardian’s review describes the film’s use of montage and poetry as an act of historical reclamation.

image.caption: A still from A Fidai Film.

sources.originalTitle: A Fidai Film review – Palestinian collage film transforms suppressed footage into works of art

segments.body: A Fidai Film builds a collage from archival material that once belonged to the Palestine Research Centre in Beirut. Israeli forces seized the archive in 1982; the review says many of the documents are believed to remain in the Israeli army’s hands. Aljafari’s film assembles footage marked by scratches, grain and pixelation, placing images from different periods into visual conversation.

segments.title: Changing the captions
segments.body: The film also covers pejorative captions placed on some reels by Israeli authorities with red paint, replacing them with excerpts from Palestinian poetry, including work by Ghassan Kanafani. The review sees these choices as more than stylistic: they return context and humanity to images shaped by suppression and historical erasure.

content.headline: Deadline turns a school suicide threat into an indictment of authoritarianism
content.shortHeadline: Deadline turns school surveillance into a political thriller
content.standfirst: Kiwi Chow’s Taiwan-set drama follows the shockwaves after a student threatens suicide unless an elite school changes its rules. The Guardian review reads its thriller plot as an indictment of surveillance, bullying and a wider institutional malaise.

image.caption: A still from Deadline.

sources.originalTitle: Deadline review – shocking threat sends tremors through authoritarian school

segments.body: Deadline is set inside a prestigious high school where pupils are tracked by AI recognition systems and ranked by academic and disciplinary scores. The story begins when an anonymous student threatens to take their life unless the school changes its authoritarian practices, sending the administration and students into turmoil.

segments.title: A system, not just individuals
segments.body: The review says the film treats bullying, self-harm and drug use as evidence of systemic problems rather than isolated failings. Chow uses the structure of a whodunnit to advance an anti-authoritarian argument, which the critic connects to his earlier documentary about the Hong Kong protests. The review notes that both films are banned in Hong Kong.

content.headline: Digger’s box-office collapse sharpens debate over Tom Cruise’s eco-satire
content.shortHeadline: Digger’s box-office collapse meets sharply divided reviews
content.standfirst: Early estimates put Digger’s global takings far below the reported cost of making and marketing it. The film has also split critics: one review praises its audacious environmental satire, while others find it shallow or hampered by Cruise’s star persona.

image.caption: Tom Cruise in Digger (2026).

sources.originalTitle: Digger on course for $245m loss after box office collapse
Digger review: Tom Cruise takes the 'biggest risk of his career' in this 'love-it-or-hate-it' folly ★★★★☆
Tom Cruise has forgotten how to act

segments.body: Digger’s reported North American box office fell sharply in its second weekend, and Variety estimates a worldwide final total of about $50m. The Guardian reports that Variety’s cost estimates imply a potential loss of roughly $245m; Warner Bros gives a lower break-even estimate of $300m, against Variety’s estimate of about $350m.

segments.title: A film critics disagree about
segments.body: The Guardian reports sharply divided reactions to Alejandro G Iñárritu’s eco-satire. The BBC review calls it an eccentric, politically blunt folly whose excesses are part of its risk-taking; the Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw calls it shallow and laborious. An i Paper review is also critical, arguing that Cruise’s celebrity overwhelms the performance.

perspectives.body: The BBC review sees Digger’s extravagant style and Cruise’s transformation as deliberate risks, and argues that its environmental satire has become more plausible with time. It says the film’s divisiveness does not make it a failure.

segments.title: What the numbers can—and cannot—show
segments.body: The reported loss remains an estimate, not a final accounting: the available figures for production, marketing and the break-even point differ. The film’s underperformance also comes amid a difficult year for Warner Bros, while another tech-focused film, The Social Reckoning, opened below expectations, according to the Guardian report.

content.headline: Hallowarrior makes a teenage survivor the centre of its Halloween horror
content.shortHeadline: Hallowarrior turns Halloween into survival horror
content.standfirst: Ben Sottak’s feature debut follows a teenager who has survived alone since a catastrophe wiped out most of humanity. The Guardian review praises Milly Shapiro’s performance and the film’s carefully built world of cosy Halloween ritual and post-apocalyptic danger.

image.caption: Milly Shapiro in Hallowarrior.

sources.originalTitle: Hallowarrior review – apocalyptic Home Alone-style survival horror delivers inventive shocks

segments.body: In Hallowarrior, 16-year-old Pumpkin has been living alone in her rural family home since a disease killed most of humanity. She tries to keep her family’s Halloween tradition alive by broadcasting an invitation over the radio, but the message attracts people who threaten her safety.

segments.title: A grounded centre for outlandish scares
segments.body: The review praises Milly Shapiro, in her first major screen role since Hereditary, for making Pumpkin both inexperienced and resourceful. It also highlights the production design, which moves between a cosy Halloween home and a motel-like unease, giving the film’s heightened horror a plausible emotional centre.

content.headline: Black Swan became one former dancer’s unlikely comfort film
content.shortHeadline: Why Black Swan became a dancer’s comfort film
content.standfirst: A writer revisits Darren Aronofsky’s ballet nightmare, first watched as a young dancer, and finds comfort in its claustrophobic world. The essay argues that the film’s dread and delight make it a rare, repeatable indulgence.

image.caption: Natalie Portman in Black Swan.

sources.originalTitle: ‘A rare indulgence’: why Black Swan is my feelgood movie

segments.body: The writer first watched Black Swan at 12, while training to become a professional dancer, and remembers being disturbed by its intensity. Returning to the film as an adult, they find its enclosed world—Nina’s cramped home, the studio and a shadowed New York—strangely soothing.

segments.title: The pleasure in the pressure
segments.body: The essay connects that comfort to the film’s obsessive focus on artistic discipline and the physical demands of ballet. Natalie Portman’s performance, the writer argues, makes visible the pain beneath ballet’s apparent delicacy; repeated viewings preserve the story’s unsettling ambiguity rather than dulling it.

content.headline: The Influencer Project makes its Copenhagen satire uneasy viewing
content.shortHeadline: The Influencer Project turns a Copenhagen trip into a thriller
content.standfirst: Chiara King plays a version of herself in a thriller that imitates the rhythms of social-media content. The Guardian review finds its satire of influencer culture unsettling, but questions whether the film is critiquing online exploitation or using the same tactics.

image.caption: Chiara King in The Influencer Project.

sources.originalTitle: The Influencer Project review – ick-inducing thriller exploits overexposed tropes

segments.body: In The Influencer Project, Chiara King visits Copenhagen on a tourism-sponsored trip, filming her shopping, meals and a haunted-house visit for social media. Threatening messages then disrupt the polished stream of content, with the sender demanding that King stop speaking or face violence.

segments.title: Satire or participation?
segments.body: The review’s central reservation is that the film both mocks the exploitative conventions of online content and profits from reproducing them. It sees an uneasy, potentially deliberate tension in the film’s approach, but leaves open whether that makes for a sharp critique or a weak imitation of already familiar social-media tropes.

content.headline: Alex Gibney says Universal reconsidered international plans for Musk film
content.shortHeadline: Gibney says Universal wavered over international release of Musk film
content.standfirst: The director says Universal hesitated over releasing his four-hour Elon Musk documentary outside North America, while the studio maintains it has remained committed to an international release. Gibney says talks about a plan are now under way.

image.caption: Alex Gibney and Elon Musk.

sources.originalTitle: Alex Gibney says Universal ‘wavered’ over releasing Elon Musk documentary

segments.body: Alex Gibney told the New York Times that Universal “wavered” over international distribution of his documentary about Elon Musk. The Guardian reports that the film is opening in the US through Bleecker Street, while Universal holds the international rights acquired in 2023.

segments.title: Release plans remain unsettled
segments.body: A Variety report suggested legal threats from Musk concerned the studio, while Universal has said it was always committed to an international release and that its plans had not changed. Asked about the reasons for the hesitation, Gibney said, “You can walk and chew gum at the same time”; he later said discussions with Universal about a release plan were taking place.

content.headline: Treasure Island’s new TV reimagining sidelines its young hero
content.shortHeadline: Treasure Island gives Jim Hawkins a superpower—and little else
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s review takes aim at a six-part adaptation that gives Jim Hawkins an exceptional memory while shifting much of the action to his mother. David Oyelowo’s Long John Silver, the critic argues, is a commanding presence in a series that otherwise loses its way.

image.caption: David Oyelowo as Long John Silver with Tom Sweet as Jim Hawkins and Hayley Atwell as Bess.

sources.originalTitle: Treasure Island review – this TV stinker does its best to ruin a literary classic

segments.body: This six-part Treasure Island gives Jim Hawkins a near-mystical memory, which makes him the keeper of a treasure map after his mother burns the original. The Guardian review argues that the change does little to make him compelling, while his mother Bess takes a more prominent role in the early episodes.

segments.title: One performance amid the wreckage
segments.body: The review praises David Oyelowo’s Long John Silver as an explosive presence, but says he cannot rescue a story weighed down by additional plot twists and a conspicuous “magic memory” device. Its verdict is sharply negative about this reimagining, while acknowledging Oyelowo’s charisma.

content.headline: The Party turns a country-house gathering into a gleeful thriller
content.shortHeadline: The Party is a fast, wickedly entertaining country-house thriller
content.standfirst: Sarah Solemani’s adaptation of Elizabeth Day’s novel opens with a bloodstained political journalist and a party full of secrets. The Guardian review relishes the pace, the ensemble and the show’s crowded web of betrayals, even without a character to root for.

image.caption: Sarah Solemani as Lucy and Luke Evans as Martin in The Party.

sources.originalTitle: The Party review – this pacey, perfectly cast thriller is enormous fun

segments.body: The Party begins with political journalist Martin being questioned in a bloodstained shirt, then rewinds to a lavish gathering at a country house. As a political leadership contest looms, the guests’ past relationships, rivalries and private schemes start to collide.

segments.title: A ride through bad behaviour
segments.body: The review praises the series as pacey, moreish and well cast, with Lindsay Duncan singled out among the ensemble. It says the pleasure lies less in rooting for anyone than in following the mystery through its hateful characters, flashbacks and accumulating secrets.

content.headline: Bake Off’s audience-choice week adds a welcome dose of chaos
content.shortHeadline: Bake Off loosens its rules with audience-choice week
content.standfirst: Viewers, rather than judges Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood, set the challenges in a first for The Great British Bake Off. The i Paper’s critic sees the unusual tasks and sharper judge dynamic as a promising break from the show’s familiar cosiness.

image.caption: Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood on The Great British Bake Off.

sources.originalTitle: Bake Off is toughening up. Good

segments.body: Bake Off’s first audience-choice week handed challenge-setting to viewers. The bakers made cheesecakes with family members, different bakes for the technical round and wearable creations for the showstopper, including a cake shaped as a hat.

segments.title: A little less cosy
segments.body: The i Paper’s review argues that the format change brought extra tension to a show whose gentleness can feel overfamiliar. It also welcomes a sharper dynamic between Lawson and Hollywood, while cautioning that Bake Off need not become hostile television to keep its edge.

content.headline: Richard Armitage on Winter, private life and an improvised pillow scene
content.shortHeadline: Richard Armitage on Winter and keeping a private life
content.standfirst: The actor discusses his new ITV crime drama, his attraction to darker roles and the limits of what performers owe the public. He also explains that his infamous pillow scene in Obsession was intended to be degrading, not erotic.

image.caption: Richard Armitage.

sources.originalTitle: Winter’s Richard Armitage: ‘My pillow humping scene was improvised’

segments.body: Richard Armitage plays forensic pathologist Ethan Winter in ITV’s new case-of-the-week crime drama. He describes the character’s teasing relationship with detective DI Bell as a source of humour, even as Winter’s confidence can become patronising. Armitage says the pillow scene in Netflix’s Obsession was improvised to show a man’s behaviour becoming tragic and degrading, not sexy.

segments.title: The case for privacy
segments.body: Armitage says he values the idea of a private life and questions the pressure on younger generations to turn everything into content. He also distinguishes actors, who may disappear into roles, from movie stars who project versions of themselves on screen. The interview touches on his bisexuality, writing and work as an audiobook narrator.

content.headline: Strictly’s early exit for Amy Dowden exposes the risks of pairing
content.shortHeadline: Amy Dowden’s early Strictly exit raises questions about its pairings
content.standfirst: The i Paper’s critic argues that Amy Dowden’s second consecutive first-week exit is unfair to a popular professional who has faced years of disruption on the show. The piece uses her departure to examine how celebrity-professional pairings shape Strictly’s appeal.

image.caption: Amy Dowden on Strictly Come Dancing.

sources.originalTitle: Amy Dowden’s exit exposes one big Strictly problem

segments.body: Amy Dowden has left Strictly Come Dancing in the first week for a second year running, paired with celebrity hairdresser Chris Appleton. The i Paper argues that the pairing gave the professional dancer little chance to progress, following earlier years disrupted by a partner’s controversy, an injury and her cancer treatment.

segments.title: Why the professionals matter
segments.body: The column argues that viewers often invest in the professional dancers and their partnerships more than the celebrity contestants. It sees Dowden as a particularly important part of Strictly’s sense of community, and says she deserved a series defined by her skill as a teacher and performer rather than by her resilience through illness.

content.headline: Kerry Washington’s new podcast takes celebrities back to their hometowns
content.shortHeadline: Kerry Washington’s podcast asks stars about where they grew up
content.standfirst: Kerry Washington’s web series has become a podcast in which guests talk about the places that shaped them. This week’s recommendations also include family-history reporting, a Spice Girls series and a close look at the James Webb telescope.

image.caption: Kerry Washington hosts Street You Grew Up On.

sources.originalTitle: Kerry Washington takes A-listers back to the streets they grew up on: best podcasts of the week

segments.body: Street You Grew Up On, now a podcast hosted by Kerry Washington, invites guests to revisit the places where they were raised. Ben Affleck is the first guest, discussing his childhood in Cambridge, Massachusetts, his parents’ divorce and a mugging he had not told his mother about.

segments.title: More listening picks
segments.body: The Guardian’s weekly selection also recommends a family-history podcast by comedian Hunter Hill, Rosie Ramsey’s series on the Spice Girls and Maggie Aderin’s account of the James Webb Space Telescope. A daily podcast will also report on Russell Brand’s trial and explore the role of social media in high-profile cases.

content.headline: Tonight on TV: British Muslims reflect on life after 9/11
content.shortHeadline: Tonight: British Muslims on life after 9/11
content.standfirst: A documentary by Mobeen Azhar and Masood Khan looks at how the attacks changed life for British Muslims, including the film-makers’ own experiences. Tonight’s listings also include reporting on Roman Abramovich and the documentary Killing Anna.

image.caption: Mobeen Azhar and Masood Khan in their documentary.

sources.originalTitle: TV tonight: how did 9/11 affect the experience of being Muslim in Britain?

segments.body: In a BBC Two documentary, journalists Mobeen Azhar and Masood Khan explore how 9/11 changed the experience of being Muslim in Britain. Azhar says the community had once been visible in public life and asks how the attacks continue to shape that experience 25 years later.

segments.title: Other programmes tonight
segments.body: The Guardian’s listings also point to a Panorama investigation of documents concerning Roman Abramovich’s wealth; he disputes the allegations and denies wrongdoing. Later, Channel 4 airs Killing Anna, about researcher Annsar Shahhoud’s use of a false Facebook identity to gather evidence from Syrian officials and militia about massacres.

content.headline: Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil film recreates the feeling of playing the games
content.shortHeadline: Resident Evil’s new film recreates the fear of playing
content.standfirst: Rather than rely on familiar heroes, Zach Cregger’s adaptation follows an ordinary courier through a world of limited ammunition, scattered clues and escalating danger. The Guardian argues that it captures the games’ distinctive sense of vulnerability.

image.caption: Zach Cregger on the set of Resident Evil with actor Austin Abrams.

sources.originalTitle: How Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil stands out from all other game adaptations

segments.body: The Guardian’s games column argues that Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil adaptation is faithful to the series despite leaving out familiar characters such as Leon, Claire and Ada Wong. Its central figure is courier Bryan Hodukavich, who is caught in an outbreak with little equipment and limited knowledge of what is happening.

segments.title: The mechanics of fear
segments.body: The film draws on recognisable game structures: locations that include a farmhouse, tunnel, hospital and sewer; clues delivered through recordings and brief exchanges; and weapons that improve as ammunition remains scarce. The writer says the adaptation recreates the experience of moving through an unfamiliar world, rather than simply translating the games’ plot and characters.

content.headline: Gears of War: E-Day has thrilling combat but too little else
content.shortHeadline: Gears of War: E-Day’s combat shines in a repetitive prequel
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s review praises the prequel’s fluid combat and destructible environments but finds its long, repetitive levels and scattered collectibles frustrating. Its strongest action, the critic says, is not enough to make the whole game feel adventurous.

image.caption: Marcus in Gears of War: E-Day.

sources.originalTitle: Gears of War: E-Day review – an alien invasion shouldn’t be this boring

segments.body: Gears of War: E-Day revisits the alien invasion that launched the series’ central conflict, following Marcus Fenix and his squad through the early days of the attack. The review says combat feels better than in earlier entries, with more fluid movement, weighty weapons and environments that break apart during fights.

segments.title: A prequel that goes in circles
segments.body: The review criticises repeated routes through the same areas, large levels crowded with collectibles and objectives that punish players for straying from the intended path. It argues that the game’s best horror moments are too rare to balance out the repetition, leaving a strong combat system surrounded by an experience that does not build on its early ideas.

content.headline: A trip through mobile-game ads becomes an unsettling gaming feature
content.shortHeadline: A mobile-game ad rabbit hole turns disturbing
content.standfirst: A Guardian writer downloads a string of cheap phone games after watching their ads, only to encounter misleading claims, forced waits and increasingly disturbing promotions. The feature connects one frustrating experiment to the attention economy around free-to-play games.

image.caption: A screenshot of the Annoying Uncle Punch mobile game.

sources.originalTitle: Help! I have disappeared down a rabbithole of horrible mobile gaming adverts

segments.body: Trying to use short mobile-game sessions as a break from a difficult period, the writer follows ads from one free-to-play game to another. Some advertised features are absent from the games themselves, while others require players to watch long ads to keep playing or revive a character.

segments.title: The cost of “free”
segments.body: The promotions become increasingly unsettling, moving from games to gambling apps, supposed cash rewards, dating assistants and products aimed at older people. The writer describes being unable to skip or dismiss some adverts and sees the experience as a grim version of the attention economy, rather than the brief distraction they had wanted.

content.headline: Roman fort in Wales may give a medieval emperor’s legend a historical basis
content.shortHeadline: Roman fort may link Welsh legend to Magnus Maximus
content.standfirst: Coins and other finds at a newly identified fort in Pembrokeshire suggest there may be a historical basis for a medieval tale placing the Roman emperor Magnus Maximus in the area. They do not establish that he was there.

image.caption: Mock-up showing the Roman fort site in the Preseli Hills, Pembrokeshire.

sources.originalTitle: Roman fort found in Wales could prove myth of emperor’s camp is real

segments.body: Archaeologists have identified a Roman fort near Frenni Fawr in Pembrokeshire, where the medieval Welsh tale The Dream of Macsen Wledig places the emperor Magnus Maximus. The excavation has uncovered late fourth-century coins, Roman tiles and pottery, among other evidence of a military site.

segments.title: What the finds suggest
segments.body: The fort, discovered in 2024, measures about 180 by 150 metres and may have housed around 500 troops. Archaeologist Mark Merrony says its position and the finds could help explain the tale’s connection to the area. The evidence points to a Roman military presence; it does not show that Magnus Maximus personally camped there.

content.headline: UK report warns rising ADHD diagnoses could bring risk of overdiagnosis
content.shortHeadline: UK report flags possible overdiagnosis as ADHD diagnoses rise
content.standfirst: A government-commissioned review says diagnosis rates for ADHD and autism are approaching or exceeding estimated prevalence in some groups. It warns of growing risks, but says the evidence does not establish widespread overdiagnosis.

sources.originalTitle: The four reasons why ADHD experts fear the UK is heading towards overdiagnosis

segments.body: A UK government-commissioned report has warned that rapidly rising ADHD and autism diagnoses may increase the risk of overdiagnosis. In England, the share of teenage boys diagnosed with ADHD rose from 2% to 5% in a decade; among girls of the same age, it rose from 0.5% to 2.5%. The report says diagnosis rates are approaching or, for some groups, already exceeding population prevalence estimates.

segments.title: A warning, not a verdict
segments.body: The report says the available research does not, by itself, show that overdiagnosis is already happening at scale. It identifies factors that may affect rates, including broader diagnostic definitions, increased awareness and subjective assessments without a definitive test. Experts also caution that underdiagnosis and misdiagnosis remain concerns, and that rising numbers alone cannot determine who has received an incorrect diagnosis.

content.headline: UK police unit ends Palantir software trial after two years
content.shortHeadline: Police unit ends Palantir AI software trial
content.standfirst: An East Midlands organised-crime unit will not renew its Palantir contract after a two-year trial. It says funding and its assessment of what the software could deliver informed the decision; it has not disclosed how the system was used.

image.caption: Palantir technology has been tested by several UK police forces.

sources.originalTitle: Police unit pulls plug on Palantir AI technology

segments.body: The East Midlands Special Operations Unit, which investigates serious crime across five counties, has decided not to fund a new contract for Palantir’s Foundry software after a trial that began in October 2024. The unit says Palantir must now show it has disconnected from its systems and deleted its data. It confirmed that the trial used data from Leicestershire Police but declined to identify the datasets or explain how the software was used.

segments.title: Scrutiny over public use
segments.body: The unit said its decision followed an assessment of what the software could deliver and its future funding; it also said the trial had checks, balances and independent review. Palantir says its software has helped other UK forces and that customers control how it is used. Critics have raised concerns about surveillance and the company’s work for the Israeli military and US immigration enforcement; Amnesty International UK welcomed the decision to end the trial.

content.headline: UK warns AI breach is likely as Microsoft calls for binding safety rules
content.shortHeadline: UK warns of likely AI breach as Microsoft urges safety rules
content.standfirst: The UK’s AI minister says a breach of national cyber defences is likely or inevitable and outlines work to prepare. Microsoft president Brad Smith is separately urging global rules, including incident reporting and safeguards to halt out-of-control systems.

image.caption: UK AI minister Kanishka Narayan has warned that the country’s cyber defences could be breached.

sources.originalTitle: Cyber-attack like OpenAI Medicare breach ‘seems likely’ in UK, says minister
AI minister warns 'likely' UK's cyber defences will be breached
AI is less regulated than milk, says Microsoft president
AI less regulated than milk, Microsoft president says in warning over safety
Microsoft president says UK is best placed to drive AI regulation

segments.body: The UK’s AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, says it is “likely, if not inevitable” that the country’s cyber defences will be breached. He pointed to the OpenAI agent incident in Australia and said the government is working to strengthen protections. Existing pilots have identified and fixed more than 1,000 vulnerabilities across government systems, according to the BBC; the government also says the UK’s AI Security Institute is evaluating the latest models before release.

segments.title: Calls for stronger oversight
segments.body: Microsoft president Brad Smith has called for global AI safety rules, including a legal duty to report incidents affecting victims, independent evaluation of some products before release and ways to pause systems that become uncontrollable. He says voluntary commitments are not enough to address risks from less responsible companies. His call comes amid a contrast with US President Donald Trump’s preference for industry self-regulation.

perspectives.body: TechCrunch reports that Smith views the UK as better placed than the US or EU to lead on rules, citing the UK’s access to leading models for safety testing. He also says a recent voluntary industry pledge is a necessary first step, but not sufficient.

content.headline: Manchester City beat Liverpool 3-0 at Anfield as financial case looms
content.shortHeadline: City beat Liverpool 3-0 amid financial-case uncertainty
content.standfirst: Erling Haaland, Jeremy Doku and Rayan Cherki scored in a commanding City win, their first match since an independent commission found the club had breached financial rules. City have appealed, and sanctions are yet to be announced.

image.caption: Liverpool fans display their opposition to Manchester City at Anfield.

sources.originalTitle: Man City's statement win has feeling of irrelevance with season in limbo
Manchester City
Winless and an 'easy touch' - what's happened to the Anfield fear factor?

segments.body: Manchester City won 3-0 at Anfield, with second-half goals from Erling Haaland, Jeremy Doku and Rayan Cherki. Liverpool played the final half-hour with 10 men after Ryan Gravenberch was sent off; City took the lead through Haaland shortly afterwards.

segments.title: A victory under a cloud
segments.body: The match was City's first since an independent commission found the club guilty of breaches of Premier League financial rules. City have appealed and sanctions have not been announced, leaving the consequences for the club and the league unresolved.

perspectives.body: BBC Sport's Liverpool analysis says the defeat extended the club's run without a Premier League home win to five matches, dating back to last season. It also notes that Liverpool have scored only twice in three home league games this season.

content.headline: Grant Forrest wins Spanish Open and earns places at The Open and Masters
content.shortHeadline: Forrest wins Spanish Open to qualify for The Open and Masters
content.standfirst: The Scot birdied the 72nd hole to finish one shot clear of Eugenio Chacarra and Victor Perez. The victory earns Forrest a place at next year's The Open and Masters.

image.caption: Grant Forrest celebrates his birdie at the 72nd hole that secured the Spanish Open.

sources.originalTitle: Forrest earns major invites with Spanish Open win

segments.body: Grant Forrest made a birdie at the last to win the Spanish Open by one shot. He finished 14 under par, ahead of home favourite Eugenio Chacarra and Victor Perez, who shared second. It was Forrest's third DP World Tour title and his first professional win outside Scotland.
The win also secures Forrest places at The Open and the Masters next year. He said he was in "pure shock" and described the prospect of going to Augusta as hard to take in.

content.headline: Zheng Qinwen wins China Open to become its first Chinese champion
content.shortHeadline: Zheng makes history with China Open victory
content.standfirst: The wildcard beat fourth seed Mirra Andreeva in straight sets in Beijing, saving three set points in the opening set. The WTA 1000 title ends a two-year title drought after a difficult period with injury and form.

image.caption: Zheng Qinwen celebrates her China Open final victory over Mirra Andreeva.

sources.originalTitle: Karaoke-singing Zheng makes history with China Open win

segments.body: Zheng Qinwen beat Mirra Andreeva 7-5, 6-4 to become the first Chinese woman to win the China Open. Ranked 54th and playing as a wildcard, Zheng saved three set points in the first set before recovering from early deficits in both sets to take the title.

It was Zheng's first WTA 1000 title and her sixth overall, ending a two-year wait for a title after a year affected by elbow surgery, fitness problems and inconsistent form. She is set to rise 31 places to 23rd in the rankings.

content.headline: Eliud Kipchoge, 41, sets Melbourne Marathon course record
content.shortHeadline: Kipchoge sets Melbourne course record at 41
content.standfirst: The two-time Olympic champion won in 2:09:10 for his 17th career marathon victory. Kipchoge said he believes his body is still peaking as he competes alongside a younger generation.

image.caption: Eliud Kipchoge wins the Melbourne Marathon in a course-record time.

sources.originalTitle: Kipchoge, 41, breaks course record at Melbourne Marathon

segments.body: Eliud Kipchoge won the Melbourne Marathon in a course-record time of two hours, nine minutes and 10 seconds. The 41-year-old Kenyan finished ahead of Australia's Thomas do Canto, who was second in 2:10:35, and Reece Edwards, third.

It was Kipchoge's 17th career win over the marathon distance and his first since the 2023 Berlin Marathon. He said he believed his body was "still peaking" and described the race as part of a world tour aiming to run a marathon on all seven continents.

content.headline: Celtic beat Motherwell as Jota returns after almost 18 months out
content.shortHeadline: Celtic win and welcome Jota back after 18 months
content.standfirst: A 2-0 victory ended Celtic's three-match losing run and lifted them back to the top of the Scottish Premiership. Jota came on in the second half for his first appearance since a long-term injury.

image.caption: Jota celebrates with Celtic fans after returning from injury.

sources.originalTitle: Jota comeback helps Celtic lift gloom in strong response

segments.body: Celtic beat Motherwell 2-0, with Camilo Duran scoring early and Benjamin Nygren adding a second after the break. The result ended a run of three defeats and returned Martin O'Neill's side to the top of the Scottish Premiership.

segments.title: Jota's return
segments.body: Winger Jota came on as a 74th-minute substitute, returning after almost 18 months out with a cruciate ligament injury. He said he had been waiting a long time to play again and was ready to help the team.

content.headline: Christian Wade reaches 100 Premiership tries in Newcastle defeat
content.shortHeadline: Wade hits 100 Prem tries despite Newcastle defeat
content.standfirst: The Newcastle winger scored a hat-trick in a 34-28 loss at Exeter, becoming only the second player to reach 100 Premiership tries. He is now one short of Chris Ashton's record.

image.caption: Christian Wade scores the try that brings him to 100 Premiership tries.

sources.originalTitle: Wade scores 100th Prem try as Newcastle lose to Exeter

segments.body: Christian Wade scored three tries as Newcastle Red Bulls lost 34-28 away to Exeter. His third, early in the second half, took him to 100 Premiership tries. Only Chris Ashton has scored more, with a record 101.

Exeter secured their first win of the season with a late penalty from Henry Slade and a try by Bachuki Tchumbadze. Wade's milestone came in a narrow defeat for Newcastle, who are second from bottom and have two losing bonus points.

content.headline: Marco Bezzecchi wins in Indonesia as Jorge Martin retakes MotoGP lead
content.shortHeadline: Bezzecchi wins as Martin takes MotoGP lead
content.standfirst: Bezzecchi passed pole-sitter Raul Fernandez with nine laps remaining. Third place moved Martin two points clear of Marc Marquez with five grands prix left.

image.caption: Marco Bezzecchi and Jorge Martin race for Aprilia at the Indonesian Grand Prix.

sources.originalTitle: Bezzecchi wins as Martin retakes championship lead

segments.body: Marco Bezzecchi won the Indonesian Grand Prix after passing Raul Fernandez with nine laps to go. Fernandez finished second, with Jorge Martin third to complete a podium sweep for Aprilia riders.

Martin's third place put him back on top of the championship standings with 355 points, two ahead of Marc Marquez, who finished sixth. Bezzecchi is third on 309 points, with five grands prix remaining.

content.headline: Australia take control against South Africa after bowling them out for 284
content.shortHeadline: Australia seize Test advantage after dismissing South Africa
content.standfirst: Australia's pace quartet and Nathan Lyon reduced the hosts from 82-1 to 284 in Durban. Steve Smith took three catches, including two off Lyon, and Australia ended day three 139 ahead.

image.caption: Steve Smith takes his 223rd Test catch, moving three clear of Joe Root among non-wicketkeepers.

sources.originalTitle: Australia veterans shine against South Africa

segments.body: Australia took control of the first Test in Durban by dismissing South Africa for 284, in reply to 390. Pat Cummins took three wickets, while Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon claimed two each. Australia closed day three on 33-0, leading by 139.

segments.title: Smith's contribution in the field
segments.body: Steve Smith took three catches, including two close-range catches off Lyon, to reach 223 in Test cricket—the most by a non-wicketkeeper, three ahead of Joe Root. Australia now have time to press their advantage across the final two days, though bad light had again shortened play.
